title: Comparative efficacy and safety of first-line therapies for advanced HER2-negative gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract: First-line regimens incorporating immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), adoptive cell therapy (ACT), and targeted agents have expanded treatment options for advanced HER2-negative gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, but their comparative efficacy and safety remain uncertain. We searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and major conference proceedings for randomized controlled trials published from 2013 to the prespecified cutoff of August 6, 2025. Frequentist network meta-analysis evaluated overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), response, disease control, and treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs). Twenty-nine trials (14,318 patients; 18 treatment nodes) were included. Anti-PD-1 plus doublet chemotherapy improved OS and PFS versus doublet chemotherapy, but heterogeneous PD-L1 criteria precluded CPS-specific inference. ACT plus triplet chemotherapy ranked highest for PFS (P-score, 0.9378) and objective response (SUCRA, 91.1); this node was supported by one 33-patient open-label phase II trial and is hypothesis-generating. PD-1/CTLA-4 and PD-L1/TGF-β bispecific antibodies plus doublet chemotherapy ranked first and second for OS (P-scores, 0.8640 and 0.8624). Missing grade ≥ 3 TRAE data precluded class-wide safety conclusions. Four mixed-site trials included 347 patients with esophageal adenocarcinoma (2.4%). Excluding three abstract-only trials left 15 nodes and broadly similar estimates, although excluded nodes became non-estimable and the PFS effect of triplet versus doublet chemotherapy lost statistical significance. Within the trial populations represented in this network, anti-PD-1 therapy plus doublet chemotherapy is the best-supported first-line chemoimmunotherapy strategy. The analysis cannot determine CPS-specific effects, and favorable ACT rankings require confirmation before clinical application.

title: Efficacy and safety of Disitamab Vedotin (RC48-ADC) monotherapy versus combination therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors in solid tumors: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Combining antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has emerged as a novel strategy to overcome immunotherapy resistance. This meta-analysis aims to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of Disitamab Vedotin (RC48) monotherapy versus combination therapy with ICIs in HER2-expressing advanced solid tumors, thereby validating its potential clinical benefits. We systematically searched multiple databases for relevant studies. Pooled ORs and HRs with 95% CIs were calculated for ORR (n = 320), DCR (n = 159), PFS (n = 300), OS (n = 70), and SAEs (n = 290). Seven studies involving 320 patients were included. Compared to monotherapy, the combination therapy yielded significantly superior efficacy, improving ORR (OR = 0.33, p < 0.05), DCR (OR = 0.42, p < 0.05), and, importantly, prolonging OS (HR = 0.46, p < 0.05). There was no statistically significant difference in PFS (HR = 0.91) or in the risk of grade ≥3 SAEs (OR = 0.77), indicating a manageable safety profile. Subgroup analysis highlighted that gastric cancer patients benefited most from combination therapy. The RC48-ICI combination demonstrates robust clinical advantages over monotherapy in improving tumor response and OS without exacerbating severe toxicity. Our research results provide preliminary evidence that confirms the potential synergistic efficacy of this "ADC+immunotherapy" strategy. These findings are preliminary and hypothesis-generating, and require confirmation in prospective randomized trials. PROSPERO CRD420251134291.

title: A Meta-Analysis of the Role of Esophagectomy in Stage 4 Esophageal Cancer.
abstract: Nearly 40% of new cases of esophageal cancer are diagnosed at stage 4. Esophagectomy may offer a survival benefit in highly selected patients with stage 4 esophageal cancer. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Databases including PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched. Studies reporting survival outcomes in patients with stage 4 esophageal cancer undergoing surgical resection were included. Random-effects models were used to pool 3-year overall survival (OS) and hazard ratios (HRs). Subgroup analyses were performed based on the timing of survival measurement (diagnosis vs. surgery). Eleven studies comprising 608 surgical patients were included. The pooled 3-year OS was 43% (95% confidence interval {CI}, 22%-67%) when measured from surgery and 61% (95% CI, 23%-89%) when measured from diagnosis or treatment initiation, with substantial heterogeneity (I2>80%). Pooled HR analysis of the 2 comparative studies without gastric cancer showed better survival with surgery, although the difference was not significant (HR, 0.16 [95% CI, 0.00-6.19]); a sensitivity analysis with the gastric cancer study yielded a similar estimate (HR, 0.25 [95% CI, 0.03-2.02]). Favorable prognostic factors included R0 resection, ypM0 status, lower nodal burden, response to systemic therapy, and oligometastatic disease. In highly selected patients with stage IV esophageal cancer, particularly those with oligometastatic disease and favorable response to systemic therapy, esophagectomy may be considered within a multimodal treatment strategy. These findings support a biologically driven, response-adapted approach to conversion surgery. Prospective studies are required to define its role.

title: Distinguishing Patients with Previous Helicobacter pylori Infection from Those Never Infected Using Logistic Regression and a Neural Network.
abstract: Objective Accurate assessment of Helicobacter pylori infection status is important for gastric cancer screening. Although current infection can be reliably detected using the stool antigen test (SAT) or urea breath test, distinguishing previously infected individuals from those who have never been infected using noninvasive serological markers remains challenging. This study evaluated the performance of logistic regression (LR) and a neural network (NN) in distinguishing between these two groups.Methods Data from 1,872 participants (1,101 never infected, 39 currently infected, and 732 previously infected) were analyzed. The infection status was determined based on the eradication history, endoscopic findings, and SAT results. For the primary analysis, participants who were currently infected were excluded. Birth year, sex, serum H. pylori antibody level, pepsinogen (PG) I, PG II, and PG I/II ratio were used as the predictors. The classification performance was evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation.Results The LR and NN models showed numerically similar performance, with area under the curve values of 0.85±0.02 and 0.88±0.01 (mean ± standard deviation), respectively. At a probability cutoff of 0.5, the recall for previously infected individuals was 66.8% ±3.6% for LR and 70.7% ±5.0% for NN. Lowering the cutoff to 0.4 improved the recall. At this cutoff, the recall for never-infected and previously infected individuals was 79.6% ±3.7% and 74.5% ±1.8% for LR, and 82.1% ±3.2% and 76.7% ±4.0% for NN, respectively.Conclusion NN and LR models using noninvasive clinical data showed numerically similar performance in distinguishing previously infected from never-infected individuals.

title: A Rational Computational Pipeline for the Discovery of a Potent EGF-Mimetic Ligand with In vitro Enhanced Proliferative Activity in Cancer Stem Cells.
abstract: This study developed a novel synthetic biomimetic ligand that replicates Epidermal Growth Factor (EGF) using an integrated in silico and in vitro pipeline. A fragment-based design strategy generated a virtual library, which was filtered to identify drug-like compounds with high predicted affinity for the EGFR. The lead compound, DB09210, demonstrated exceptional biomimetic properties. In human fibroblasts, it sustained cell viability comparably to fetal bovine serum. Notably, in 3D cultures of gastric cancer stem cells (GCSCs), DB09210 exhibited potent, time- and dose-dependent activity, surpassing native EGF in promoting proliferation after 7 days. The observed maintenance of CD133 + expression can be interpreted as evidence for preserved stemness, implying the compound may act as a potent functional mimetic mechanism. While its potent enrichment of cancer stem cells requires therapeutic caution, DB09210 is a powerful tool compound. Its ability to reliably expand stem cell populations under defined, serum-free conditions holds significant promise for regenerative medicine, organoid biobanking, and advanced ex vivo drug screening platforms.

title: A patient with Lynch syndrome and duodenal neuroendocrine carcinoma achieved a pathologic complete response to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy selected based on comprehensive genomic profiling.
abstract: We report a 27-year-old man with stage IV duodenal neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC) harboring microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) and high tumor mutational burden (TMB-high) status, who achieved a pathologic complete response to pembrolizumab selected based on comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP). After failure of platinum-based chemotherapy, CGP using FoundationOne CDx revealed MSI-H, TMB-high, and a pathogenic MSH2 frameshift variant, prompting second-line pembrolizumab, which produced marked tumor regression and enabled pancreaticoduodenectomy. The resected specimen showed no viable tumor in the primary lesion or lymph nodes, confirming a pathologic complete response; the patient has remained recurrence-free for 3 years. Germline testing confirmed the same MSH2 variant, establishing a diagnosis of Lynch syndrome; cascade testing identified four carrier relatives and enabled early detection of gastric cancer in a 24-year-old carrier. Duodenal NEC associated with Lynch syndrome has not been previously reported. This case illustrates the diagnostic and therapeutic value of CGP in rare gastrointestinal NEC.
journal: Virchows Archiv : an international journal of pathology

title: Development and Validation of a Novel Post-Neoadjuvant Staging System for Gastric Cancer Incorporating Tumor Regression Grade and Lymph Node Status: A Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: The AJCC 8th edition ypTNM staging system has limitations in prognostic stratification for gastric cancer (GC) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC), and tumor regression grade (TRG) may provide complementary prognostic information. This study aimed to develop a novel staging system that integrates TRG with ypN category to improve prognostic assessment in patients with GC after NAC. Patients with GC who underwent NAC followed by radical gastrectomy were retrospectively included and analyzed from two institutions. The development and external validation cohorts included 440 and 241 patients, respectively. The TRG-ypN staging system was constructed by integrating TRG with ypN status. Its prognostic performance was compared with the AJCC 8th edition ypTNM system using, AIC, BIC, time-dependent receiver operating characteristic analysis, and decision curve analysis. The TRG-ypN staging system showed clearer survival separation and a more consistent stepwise decline in 5-year Overall survival, with rates of 85.14%, 67.24%, 53.68%, 40.48% and 22.66% for TRG-ypN stages IA, IB, II, IIIA, and IIIB, respectively. In two-step multivariable Cox analyses, TRG-ypN stage remained associated with OS after adjustment in both cohorts. The TRG-ypN system also demonstrated higher time-dependent AUC values, lower AIC and BIC values, and greater net clinical benefit than AJCC ypTNM staging. The proposed TRG-ypN staging system provided improved prognostic stratification for patients with nonmetastatic GC after NAC. This staging system may help identify high-risk patients and support more individualized postoperative management.
journal: Journal of gastrointestinal surgery : official journal of the Society for Surgery of the Alimentary Tract

title: Targeting CLDN3 Enhances PD-1 Blockade Efficacy in Gastric Cancer by Disrupting the NF-κB/p65-CXCL1-PD-L1 Immune Evasion Axis.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Claudin 3 (CLDN3), a tight junction protein aberrantly expressed in multiple malignancies, has been implicated in tumor progression. However, its functional significance and therapeutic relevance in GC remain incompletely defined. Therefore, we systematically evaluated the functional role and underlying mechanisms of CLDN3 in GC using clinical cohort analysis, in vitro and in vivo experiments, immune co-culture systems, and transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. Using hybridoma technology, we also generated a monoclonal antibody against CLDN3 and assessed its antitumor efficacy, both as monotherapy and in combination with anti-PD-1 blockade, in vitro and in vivo. CLDN3 was upregulated in GC tissues and was associated with poor prognosis, aggressive clinicopathological features, and decreased intratumoral CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Mechanistically, CLDN3 activated the NF-κB pathway by promoting p65 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, thereby enhancing CXCL1 transcription and consequently driving GC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Furthermore, CLDN3 upregulated PD-L1 expression in a CXCL1-dependent manner, leading to decreased CD8+ T-cell infiltration and attenuated CD8+ T-cell-mediated tumor cell killing. Notably, the anti-CLDN3 monoclonal antibody demonstrated high binding affinity and specificity, significantly suppressed tumor growth and metastasis in vivo, and enhanced the antitumor efficacy of anti-PD-1 blockade, accompanied by increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Collectively, these findings indicate that CLDN3 promotes GC progression and immune evasion by activating the NF-κB/p65-CXCL1-PD-L1 signaling axis, and CLDN3 blockade combined with PD-1 inhibition may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for GC.

title: Declining Cost-Effectiveness of Gastric Cancer Screening Over a Decade: A Cohort Modelling Study.
abstract: The cost-utility of a mature cancer screening programme can shift as disease incidence, costs, and population risk change. We examined how these changes affected Korea's National Cancer Screening Program (NCSP) for gastric cancer by comparing two hypothetical cohorts parameterized with 2012 and 2022 conditions. Two structurally identical state-transition models simulated biennial endoscopic screening versus no organised screening in adults aged 40-79 years over a lifetime horizon, incorporating period-specific screen-detected health-state distributions, effective screening sensitivity, NCSP participation, and treatment costs. Incremental cost-utility ratios (ICURs) per quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) were calculated in period-specific prices. For cross-period comparison, incremental costs were converted to 2025 KRW, and net monetary benefit (NMB) was calculated at a willingness-to-pay threshold of KRW 50 million/QALY(USD 40,000). The ICUR increased from KRW 9.62 million/QALY(USD 7,694) in the 2012 model to KRW 48.62 million/QALY(USD 38,895) in the 2022 model, and NMB in 2025 KRW decreased from KRW 1.73 million to KRW -0.05 million per person. In 2022, the ICUR was KRW 28.20 million/QALY(USD 22,558) for men and KRW 84.37 million/QALY(USD 67,497) for women. The increase was driven mainly by a shift in the screen-detected histologic composition of neoplasia toward lower-risk non-adenomatous findings and by higher costs. The cost-effectiveness of uniform biennial endoscopic screening in Korea declined substantially between 2012 and 2022 and the 2022 results were markedly less favourable for women than for men. These findings support periodic reassessment of mature screening programmes and further evaluation of differentiated screening approaches.

title: Longitudinal remodeling of the tumor-immune microenvironment during regorafenib, nivolumab, and chemotherapy in advanced gastric cancer.
abstract: Previous studies combining the multikinase inhibitor regorafenib with a PD-1 inhibitor showed promising activity in gastric cancer. We conducted a phase 1b/2 trial (NCT05394740) of first-line regorafenib, nivolumab, and chemotherapy in 30 patients with mismatch repair-proficient gastric cancer and investigated its impact on the tumor microenvironment. The primary end point was met; 22 of 30 patients showed objective tumor response (73%; 80% confidence interval, 60.3 to 83.8). Single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing were performed on biopsy samples at baseline, during treatment, and at disease progression. The combination treatment increased tumor antigen-reactive CD8+ T cells and M1-like proinflammatory macrophages and decreased immunosuppressive and tumor-promoting populations, including activated CCR8+ regulatory T cells, LRRC15+ cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), RGS5+ pericytes, and APLN+ tip cells. At progression, LRRC15+ CAFs and APLN+ tip cells remained reduced, activated CCR8+ regulatory T cells reexpanded, and additional treatment-resistant subsets emerged, including APOC1+ lipid-associated macrophages. In murine models of acquired resistance, therapeutic targeting of these suppressive immune cell populations with antibodies against CCR8 or TREM2 in combination with PD-1 blockade restored antitumor immunity. These findings demonstrate dynamic remodeling of the tumor microenvironment and suggest potential therapeutic targets.

title: Robotic versus laparoscopic gastrectomy for gastric cancer: 5-year long-term results from a randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Despite increasing global adoption of robotic approaches, the comparative effectiveness of robotic gastrectomy versus laparoscopic gastrectomy for gastric cancer is uncertain, particularly regarding long-term oncologic outcomes. This phase III randomized controlled trial (RCT) enrolled 241 patients with resectable gastric cancer (clinical stages I-III) between April 1, 2018, and October 31, 2020. Patients were randomly assigned to undergo either robotic gastrectomy or laparoscopic gastrectomy. The primary endpoint was postoperative intra-abdominal infectious complications (previously reported). Secondary endpoints included long-term oncologic outcomes, specifically relapse-free survival, overall survival and patterns of recurrence. This study enrolled 241 patients, with 236 patients in the modified intention-to-treat population. The 5-year relapse-free survival in the modified intention-to-treat population did not significantly differ between the laparoscopic gastrectomy and robotic gastrectomy groups (69% vs. 75%). Similarly, overall survival was not significantly different between the groups (71% vs. 79%). The 5-year cumulative incidence of primary disease-specific death was comparable between the groups (16.1% vs. 11.6%). Patterns of recurrence did not differ between them. In subgroup analyses, the robotic gastrectomy group demonstrated significantly better overall survival than the laparoscopic gastrectomy group among male patients (HR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.25-0.95). Among patients that underwent distal gastrectomy, the robotic gastrectomy group showed a significantly lower cumulative incidence of primary disease-specific death than the laparoscopic gastrectomy group (HR, 0.24; 95% CI, 0.07-0.81). In this RCT, secondary endpoint analyses showed no statistically significant differences in 5-year relapse-free survival or overall survival between laparoscopic gastrectomy and robotic gastrectomy. umin.ac.jp/ctr Identifier UMIN000031536.
journal: Gastric cancer : official journal of the International Gastric Cancer Association and the Japanese Gastric Cancer Association

title: Advancing CLDN18.2-Targeted Therapies in Pancreatic Cancer: Current Clinical Development and Therapeutic Opportunities.
abstract: Pancreatic cancer (PC) continues to pose a major clinical challenge due to its aggressive nature and poor response to conventional treatments. CLDN18.2 (Claudin 18.2), a tight junction protein with highly restricted normal tissue expression, is frequently aberrantly expressed in PC, rendering it an attractive candidate for targeted therapy. The recent approval of zolbetuximab in CLDN18.2-positive gastric/gastroesophageal junction cancer has driven the exploration of CLDN18.2-targeted agents in PC. This review comprehensively summarizes the current landscape of CLDN18.2-targeted agents in PC, encompassing monoclonal antibodies, bispecific antibodies (BsAbs), antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapies. Although early-phase studies have shown encouraging clinical activity in patients with high CLDN18.2 expression, several challenges remain, including treatment-related toxicities, tumor heterogeneity, mechanisms of resistance, and biomarker-guided patient selection. Future efforts will focus on multispecific antibodies, combination strategies, personalized therapies, and expanded applications in other CLDN18.2-positive malignancies. Overall, CLDN18.2-targeted therapies represent a rapidly progressing field with significant potential to improve survival outcomes in PC.

title: A Case of Recurrent Gastric Cancer in Which Rheumatoid Arthritis and Sjögren's Syndrome Became Evident With Nivolumab.
abstract: A 59-year-old man with recurrent gastric cancer began nivolumab as third-line therapy and subsequently experienced joint pain and dry eyes. Symptoms worsened despite NSAIDs. He was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis and Sjögren's syndrome, associated with nivolumab, and was successfully treated with immunosuppressive and anti-rheumatic medications.

title: Efficacy and Safety of ramucirumab Combined With Nab-paclitaxel, Lobaplatin, and S-1 in Conversion Therapy for Unresectable Advanced Gastric Cancer: Preliminary Results of Conversion Therapy Cohort of RNPLS-01 Trial.
abstract: This single-center randomized controlled trial assessed the efficacy and safety of the ramucirumab plus nab-paclitaxel, lobaplatin, and S-1(RNPLS) regimen for conversion therapy in unresectable advanced gastric cancer. Seventy patients were equally assigned to receive either ramucirumab, nab-paclitaxel, lobaplatin, and S-1(RNPLS) therapy or nab-paclitaxel, lobaplatin, and S-1(NPLS) chemotherapy alone. Primary endpoints included pathological complete response (pCR) and secondary endpoints encompassed R0 resection rate, objective response rate (ORR), the disease control rate (DCR), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), duration of response (DOR), and adverse events (AE). Although the difference in pCR rate was statistically insignificant between the two groups, the RNPLS group achieved significantly higher ORR, DCR, and R0 resection rate. Moreover, the RNPLS regimen yielded prolonged PFS, longer duration of response, and promising preliminary OS. While hypertension occurred more frequently in the RNPLS group, the incidence of grade ≥3 AEs was low and comparable in both cohorts. This exploratory single-center randomized trial showed preliminary favorable efficacy of RNPLS regimen for conversion therapy in unresectable advanced gastric cancer with manageable toxicity. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06169410.

title: Integrative hdWGCNA and Machine-Learning Analysis Identifies Gastric Cancer Candidate Genes and Supports a Functional Role for KRT18.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is a frequently detected malignancy worldwide. This study aimed to identify epithelial cell-associated candidate genes in GC by integrating single-cell and bulk transcriptomic data and to explore their biological relevance using computational analyses, with in vitro functional assessment limited to KRT18. Multi-omics data were integrated to investigate the molecular mechanisms of GC. The single-cell data were processed using Seurat. Subsequently, CellChat was employed to analyze cell communication. The co-expression network of epithelial cells was constructed using high-dimensional WGCNA (hdWGCNA), and module hub genes were identified. Differential expression analysis was performed with Limma, and candidate genes were screened using LASSO and SVR-RFE. Compounds were computationally prioritized using Enrichr and DSigDB; molecular docking was not used as validation. Lastly, the biological function of KRT18 was examined in GC cells. Five candidate genes were identified: GPRC5A, KRT18, EPCAM, CLDN7, and CLDN4. These genes were associated with E2F TARGETS, GLYCOLYSIS, and OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION and correlated with multiple inferred immune-cell fractions. Drug-set enrichment nominated genistein as a computational candidate but did not establish direct binding or therapeutic efficacy. In vitro assays showed that KRT18 knockdown reduced the viability, migration, and invasion of GC cells. These findings nominate exploratory epithelial cell-associated candidate genes in GC and provide functional evidence for KRT18; further external validation is required before clinical application.

title: Network Pharmacology Identifies Stigmasterol as an Anti-Gastric Cancer Agent Targeting HSP90AA1 for Ubiquitin-Mediated Degradation.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a major cause of cancer mortality. We combined network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, public database analyses, and cell-based assays to investigate stigmasterol and heat shock protein 90 alpha family class A member 1 (HSP90AA1). Computational screening prioritized HSP90AA1 as a candidate target. In AGS and MKN-45 cells, stigmasterol treatment reduced cell viability and DNA synthesis, increased the proportion of Annexin V-positive cells, and decreased HSP90AA1 protein abundance. No statistically significant change in HSP90AA1 mRNA abundance was detected under the conditions tested. Increased ubiquitin signal in HSP90AA1 immunoprecipitates and attenuation of protein loss by MG-132 were consistent with proteasome involvement. Public database analyses showed higher HSP90AA1 expression in GC tissues and an association with clinical stage. These findings link stigmasterol treatment to HSP90AA1 downregulation in GC cells. Direct binding, the contribution of HSP90AA1 loss to the cellular effects, and in vivo efficacy remain to be established.

title: Reprogramming endocytic trafficking of antibody-drug conjugates to enhance tumor penetration and lysosomal delivery.
abstract: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have transformed cancer treatment; however, challenges such as heterogeneous antigen expression and inefficient intracellular delivery continue to limit their clinical efficacy. Herein, we present a novel "signal-fusion" ADC strategy in which trafficking signal peptides were genetically fused to the C-terminus of trastuzumab (Tz), an anti-HER2 antibody. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed that these peptides remained solvent-exposed and structurally stable while positioned away from the antigen-binding regions. The resulting tetravalent signal-fusion constructs (T1/T2) enhanced endocytic trafficking by increasing receptor internalization and redirecting antibody complexes to lysosomes. Accordingly, T1 and T2 conjugated with vc-MMAF or vc-MMAE exhibited significantly enhanced cytotoxicity, improved tumor infiltration, and robust bystander effects across multiple cancer cell lines. Pharmacokinetic studies indicated plasma half-lives comparable to that of Tz, along with increased intratumoral accumulation. Furthermore, T1/T2-vc-MMAF induced prolonged tumor regression without observable toxicity in breast and gastric cancer models. Collectively, these findings highlight a promising approach for enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of next-generation ADCs.
journal: Journal of controlled release : official journal of the Controlled Release Society

title: Pembrolizumab plus FLOT as neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapy in locally advanced gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancer: analysis of the FLOT cohort from the phase 3 KEYNOTE-585 study.
abstract: Results from the third interim analysis of the phase 3 KEYNOTE-585 study (NCT03221426) showed superior pathological complete response (pCR) with perioperative pembrolizumab and chemotherapy followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab versus placebo plus chemotherapy, then adjuvant placebo in locally advanced, resectable gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma; differences in event-free survival (EFS) were not statistically significant. We present results from a complementary cohort that evaluated pembrolizumab plus fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, and docetaxel (FLOT) versus placebo plus FLOT. KEYNOTE-585 is a randomized, phase 3 study conducted at 143 medical centers. Participants were randomly assigned 1 : 1 to pembrolizumab plus FLOT or placebo plus FLOT. In this exploratory cohort, the primary endpoint was safety. Post hoc exploratory endpoints included pCR rate per the Mandard scale by blinded independent central review, EFS per RECIST v1.1 by investigator, and overall survival (OS). Overall, 203 participants were randomly assigned (pembrolizumab group, n = 100; placebo group, n = 103). Median time from randomization to data cut-off (16 February 2024) was 43.8 months (range, 36.5-69.8). Grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse event rates were 72.7% and 62.1%, respectively. Treatment-related deaths occurred in three participants (3.0%) in the pembrolizumab group and one participant (1.0%) in the placebo group. The pCR rate was 17.0% [95% confidence interval (CI), 10.2-25.8] in the pembrolizumab group and 6.8% (95% CI, 2.8-13.5) in the placebo group. Median EFS was not reached (NR; 95% CI, 28.2-NR) versus 31.6 months (95% CI, 22.8-NR), respectively [hazard ratio (HR) 0.75, 95% CI 0.50-1.13]. Median OS was NR in either group (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.53-1.25); 36-month OS rates were 66.0% and 59.2%. Neoadjuvant/adjuvant pembrolizumab plus FLOT was feasible and showed an acceptable safety profile. Exploratory efficacy endpoints showed numerical trends consistent with those of the main cohort in locally advanced resectable gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma.

title: Coronary artery calcification is not associated with survival in advanced gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancer: a secondary analysis of the EXPAND trial.
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) is the clinical standard for staging of gastrointestinal cancer. Previous studies have highlighted the prognostic significance of coronary artery calcification (CAC) detected by CT in various types of cancer. However, the prognostic role of CAC scoring in gastrointestinal cancers is still unclear. The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of CT-defined CAC on overall survival (OS) in patients with advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer. CAC was semiquantitatively measured using the visual Weston method on baseline CT scans in 785 patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer from the phase III EXPAND trial. This present study is a secondary analysis of the base line CT images. In the original analysis patients were randomly assigned to first-line treatment with cisplatin/capecitabin ± cetuximab. The primary endpoint of the current subanalysis is the OS. For statistical analysis group differences were calculated using the Mann-Whitney-U test and ANOVA test. Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox regression analysis were used to test the effect of CAC on mortality. The median CAC score was 1 (IQR 0; 3). A total of 337 patients (42.9%) had no visible CAC (CAC score 0). Male patients had statistically significant higher CAC score compared to female patients (median 1 versus 0, p < 0.0001). In univariable Cox regression CAC showed no significant association with survival when analysed as a continuous value (HR: 0.99, 95% CI: 0.96-1.02, p = 0.74), and when dichotomized for absence and presence of calcification (HR:1.08, 95% CI: 0.92-1.26, p = 0.34). Similar results were identified in further subgroup analyses. CT-defined CAC scoring has no relevant prognostic impact in advanced gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancer undergoing first-line chemotherapy. The present study cannot confirm the promising results for CAC scoring in lung cancer patients.
journal: Journal of cancer research and clinical oncology

title: Deciphering molecular mechanisms of synergistic growth reduction in kinase inhibitor combinations.
abstract: Targeted kinase inhibitors often yield transient or incomplete responses because tumour cells buffer pathway blockade through signalling cross-talk, motivating synergistic drug combinations. However, it remains unclear whether synergy typically arises from engaging new signalling programs or from reinforcing the dominant effects of each monotherapy at shared downstream control points. Here we analyse two synergistic inhibitor pairs in AGS gastric adenocarcinoma cells: PI3K inhibition combined with inhibition of either MEK (MAP2K1, MAP2K2) or TAK1 (MAP3K7). Using time-resolved phosphoproteomics and transcriptomics after single-agent and combination treatment, we track signalling and transcriptional rewiring from 30 minutes to 24 h and partition combination responses into monotherapy-like versus combination-specific components. We show that global phosphorylation and gene expression changes under both combinations largely mirror those of the monotherapies, with limited evidence for uniquely engaged kinase programs. Instead, synergy concentrates at pathway convergence nodes, where combined perturbation amplifies downstream regulation of growth and survival circuitry, including transcriptional control through MYC and CREB1. Both combinations produce stronger suppression of MYC-linked proliferative programs and CREB1-associated survival signalling than either single agent, consistent with reinforced constraint on cell-fate decisions. At the transcriptional level, the combinations uniquely repress nucleotide metabolism and aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis, consistent with reduced mTOR activity. Together, these results indicate that synergistic growth inhibition can arise primarily from strengthened pathway convergence rather than recruitment of new signalling routes. Our approach provides insights into the molecular mechanisms affected by the PI3Ki-TAK1i and PI3Ki-MEKi combinations and can serve as a flexible framework for dissecting drug combination responses based on multi-omics measurements.

title: Gastric cancer biomarker testing in Japan: a second nationwide survey of testing practices and associations with testing location.
abstract: Testing for HER2, PD-L1, MSI/MMR, and CLDN18 guides first-line treatment selection for unresectable advanced or recurrent gastric cancer. Our first nationwide survey revealed substantial interinstitutional variation in HER2 and PD-L1 results and identified fixation time as one contributing factor. The present survey assessed testing timing and location and expanded the analysis to CLDN18 and MSI/MMR. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 447 institutions certified by the Japanese Gastric Cancer Association. Testing volumes, timing, and location for the four biomarkers were analyzed together with results from the previous survey. Responses were obtained from 155 institutions (34.7%). Nearly all institutions performed all four biomarker tests, and 81.9% conducted simultaneous testing before first-line therapy. In-house testing rates were 80.1% for HER2-IHC, 34.6% for CLDN18, 26.3% for MMR, 25.6% for HER2-ISH, 16.7% for PD-L1, and 9.6% for MSI. After adjustment for annual testing volume, institutions performing ISH in-house had higher odds of HER2 IHC 2 + results in surgical specimens, whereas the association did not reach statistical significance in biopsy specimens. Overall CLDN18 positivity was 38.6% and was significantly higher in institutions performing in-house testing after adjustment for testing volume. HER2 negativity correlated positively with CLDN18 positivity among institutions performing both tests in-house. Although simultaneous four-biomarker testing is widely adopted in Japan, the use of in-house versus outsourced testing varies by biomarker and institution and is associated with differences in reported positivity rates. Our findings underscore the need for continued quality assurance and standardization to ensure reliable biomarker assessment and appropriate treatment selection.
journal: Gastric cancer : official journal of the International Gastric Cancer Association and the Japanese Gastric Cancer Association

title: [Minimally invasive and robotic gastrectomy].
abstract: Evidence from Asia demonstrates that minimally invasive gastrectomy can be safely performed for early-stage gastric cancer, with advantages at least in the early postoperative course; however, these data have limited transferability to Europe, where locally advanced stages predominate and are treated within multimodal concepts. Robotic-assisted systems have further expanded the technical spectrum. Is minimally invasive or robotic gastrectomy safely feasible in Europe for locally advanced stages or does it remain a procedure for specialized centers? Randomized trials confirm the oncological equivalence of laparoscopic gastrectomy with consistent perioperative advantages, at least for early stages of cancer. Asian studies also demonstrate benefits of minimally invasive procedures for locally advanced stages, whereas European data do not consistently confirm these advantages. For robotic gastrectomy, first randomized controlled trials (RCT) demonstrate comparable short-term outcomes; technical advantages are discussed particularly in anatomically demanding situations. Initial studies also suggest potential benefits of robotic over laparoscopic gastrectomy in terms of disease-free survival. The evidence derives predominantly from Asian cohorts with limited transferability to western patients. In specialized centers with adequate case volumes, minimally invasive gastrectomy can today be safely performed even in locally advanced stages and as part of multimodal treatment concepts. Convincing evidence for the superiority of minimally invasive procedures does not, however, currently exist for this patient group. Robotic surgery complements the surgical spectrum; whether the oncological advantages suggested by initial studies will prove robust cannot be conclusively assessed at this time.

title: Preclinical Study of the 89Zr/177Lu-Labeled Engineered VHH-based Antibody for CLDN18.2-Targeted Radiotheranostics.
abstract: Claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2) is a tight junction protein aberrantly expressed in gastric and pancreatic cancer. In this study, we developed the novel nanobody 18.2-50H and VHH-Fc fusion antibody 18.2-50C radiolabeled with 89Zr/177Lu for CLDN18.2-targeted radiotheranostics. Zolbetuximab (IMAB362), 18.2-50H, and 18.2-50C were conjugated with DFO and labeled with 89Zr, respectively. Radiochemical purity and in vitro stability were determined by radio-TLC. CLDN18.2-targeting specificity was evaluated using HEK-293T and HEK-293T/CLDN18.2 cells. PET/CT imaging and biodistribution studies were performed in mouse models and cynomolgus monkeys. Subsequently, 177Lu-DOTA-18.2-50C was prepared and assessed for tumor targeting in gastric cancer PDX models. 89Zr-DFO-IMAB362, 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50H, and 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50C were prepared with satisfactory radiochemical yield, specific activity, and stability. Tumors were clearly visible as early as 1 h post-injection of 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50H, with an uptake value of 9.07 ± 2.36 %ID/g and a tumor-to-muscle ratio of 27.35 ± 3.72. Fc-fused 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50C exhibited improved retention and higher tumor uptake than 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50H and 89Zr-DFO-IMAB362, with % ID/g increasing continuously from 5.07 ± 0.29 at 1 h to 32.95 ± 1.57 at 168 h. Notably, the introduction of the Fc chain also markedly increased the radiation exposure in the liver and spleen. Consistently, PET imaging in cynomolgus showed that 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50C is mainly concentrated in the liver, but no apparent abnormality was observed. Furthermore, 177Lu-DOTA-18.2-50C presented remarkable tumor selectivity with prolonged retention (16.92 ± 1.94 % ID/g at 5 d post-injection) in PDX models. Nanobody 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50H demonstrated a superior tumor-to-background ratio, positioning it as a promising tracer for detecting CLDN18.2-overexpressing lesions. 89Zr/177Lu-labeled VHH-Fc antibody 18.2-50C exhibited sustained higher tumor uptake than commercially available IMAB362 and provides a novel potential candidate for CLDN18.2-targeted radionuclide therapy.

title: First-in-Human PET/CT Imaging of FXX489, a Second-Generation Cyclic Peptide FAP Inhibitor: A Translational Exploratory Study.
abstract: Sufficient tumor uptake and retention, and high tumor-to-kidney ratio are highly relevant for fibroblast activation protein (FAP)-targeted tracers as imaging companions for theranostic development. Although FAP-2286 improves tumor retention versus early-generation FAPI tracers, its extended renal residence limits its application as a radiopharmaceutical therapy. We benchmarked FXX489, a next-generation cyclic peptide FAP ligand, against FAP-2286 preclinically and evaluated first-in-human [68Ga]Ga-FXX489 PET/CT to support its translational development for FAP-directed theranostics. [68Ga]Ga-FXX489 showed stronger FAP affinity than [68Ga]Ga-FAP-2286, including higher cellular uptake, lower efflux, and lower IC50. In HT-1080-hFAP xenografts, [68Ga]Ga-FXX489 achieved higher tumor uptake and retention on micro-PET and ex vivo biodistribution, and a higher tumor-to-kidney ratio. In patients (n = 10), [68Ga]Ga-FXX489 was well tolerated, and detected all 12 primary lesions (mean SUVmax, 11.20 ± 3.24) and all 42 metastatic lymph nodes (100% [42/42] vs 74% [31/42] for [18F]FDG, P < 0.001), while visualizing gastric cancer lesions with higher uptake than [18F]FDG in a paired comparison. [68Ga]Ga-FXX489 improves tumor retention and tumor-to-kidney ratio compared to [68Ga]Ga-FAP-2286 while maintaining specific FAP targeting. First-in-human [68Ga]Ga-FXX489 PET/CT shows promising detection of primary and metastatic lesions, supporting further clinical applications.

title: Agreement Between Medical Laboratory Technologists and Pathologists' Assessment of ERBB2 (HER2) Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization Across Breast and Gastric Scoring Criteria.
abstract: ERBB2 (HER2) fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) guides therapy selection for solid tumors, including breast and gastric cancers. While laboratory technologists typically perform the initial enumeration of HER2 FISH, laboratories differ in the extent of pathologist review, ranging from full slide reassessment to review of representative captured images. By performing a retrospective analysis of ∼10,000 HER2 FISH cases scored using breast and gastric criteria, the objective was to define decision boundaries at which technologists' and pathologists' interpretations converge, enabling a data-driven approach to triaging HER2 FISH sign-out. Results showed that agreement between technologists' and pathologists' interpretations was highest when technologists' counts were well beyond the diagnostic cutoffs for the HER2/CEP17 ratio and the number of HER2 signals per cell. Conversely, cases near diagnostic thresholds showed increased discordance, emphasizing the need for full review of the FISH slide in this subset. Individual technologists differed in their percent discordance with pathologists' final results; however, this was not explained by case volume (experience) alone and did not consistently improve over time. In summary, distinct HER2 FISH technologists HER2/CEP17 ratio and HER2 signal number per cell values were identified where concordance with pathologists results exceeded 99%, suggesting cases in these ranges may require only limited pathologist slide review, potentially allowing for more efficient triaging and sign-out of HER2 FISH.

title: Spatial Organization of Tumor-Infiltrating B Cells Informs Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Response in Claudin 18.2-Expressing Gastric Cancer.
abstract: Claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2), a tight junction protein normally expressed in the gastric epithelium and rendered accessible during malignant transformation, has emerged as a key therapeutic target. Here, we seek to characterize the immune microenvironment of CLDN18.2-expressing gastric cancer and identify immune features associated with CLDN18.2 expression status. Tumor-immune features were profiled in 103 patients with HER2-neg/low advanced gastric cancer treated with first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) using multiplex immunohistochemistry [7,423,483 cells across 2,315 regions of interest (ROI)]. The findings were validated in five published whole-transcriptome sequencing/microarray cohorts (1,521 samples), including the landmark CheckMate 649 phase III trial. Spatial immune architecture was assessed by cellular neighborhood analysis. Digital spatial profiling (DSP) was performed on 480 ROIs from a CLDN18.2-annotated tissue microarray (75 patients). CLDN18.2high tumors showed reproducible enrichment of humoral pathways, with higher CD20+ B-cell density and enrichment of B-cell/plasma-cell signatures. CLDN18.2 status alone was not associated with response or survival on first-line ICI therapy; in CLDN18.2low tumors, B-cell enrichment was associated with ICI benefit, unlike CLDN18.2high tumors. Spatial analyses indicated that CLDN18.2high tumors preferentially harbored tumor-infiltrating B cells, rather than tertiary lymphoid structure/lymphoid aggregate-like neighborhoods, and this tumor-compartment localization was associated with diminished ICI benefit. DSP confirmed that CD20+ B-cell enrichment was most pronounced within tumor regions, alongside compartment-specific activation of humoral and extrafollicular response programs and interferon-associated and remodeling signatures. CLDN18.2high gastric cancer exhibits a humoral-enriched microenvironment with increased tumor-infiltrating B cells and spatial immune organization associated with reduced ICI benefit. Spatial and humoral-state biomarkers may inform ongoing CLDN18.2-directed combination trials.
journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research

title: Lack of Usefulness of Literature-Based Helicobacter pylori Resistance Data for Predicting First-Line Empirical Treatment Effectiveness in the European Registry on H. pylori Management (Hp-EuReg).
abstract: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection causes gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, and gastric cancer. Without an effective vaccine, eradication therapy remains crucial. However, increasing antibiotic resistance compromises treatment effectiveness. To evaluate whether literature-based resistance data could predict first-line empirical treatment effectiveness. Resistance rates for clarithromycin, metronidazole, and levofloxacin were extracted from bibliographic reviews and estimated for three timeframes: the treatment year, the preceding year, and the last five years average. These rates (2008-2024) were matched with outcomes from the European Registry on H. pylori Management (Hp-EuReg, WorldHpReg partner), a prospective real-world study involving 40 countries. Analyses included Spearman's correlations, multivariate logistic regressions adjusted for demographic, clinical, and therapeutic-related variables, bootstrap resampling stratified by eradication success, and Random Forest models. Analysis included 37,659 patients receiving first-line empirical treatment from 13 countries. Moderate negative correlations were observed between metronidazole and clarithromycin resistances for some regimens. In the regression model, including either contemporaneous or previous-year resistance rates, clarithromycin resistance showed a negligible positive association, while metronidazole resistance was negatively associated. In regimen-specific models, previous-year clarithromycin resistance was positively associated with success in concomitant therapy, whereas higher five-year mean clarithromycin resistance reduced eradication odds in quadruple clarithromycin-amoxicillin-bismuth therapy. Random Forest models identified compliance, proton-pump inhibitor dose, regimen duration, and treatment as the strongest predictors of eradication, while resistance variables contributed minimally. Literature-based resistance data are not useful for guiding real-world first-line H. pylori therapy, highlighting the need for individualized antibiotic susceptibility testing to obtain reliable resistance information. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02328131.

title: Precise unidirection delivery and site-specific release utilizing a nanocapsules-loaded mucoadhesive in situ gel: Targeted eradication of Helicobacter pylori and gastric homeostasis restoration.
abstract: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection disrupts the gastric microenvironment and promotes the development of gastric cancer and other gastrointestinal diseases. Despite the high prevalence of asymptomatic chronic infection and recurrent infections, persistent mucosal injury continues to drive early pathological alterations, including gastric epithelial remodeling and intestinal metaplasia, that may become irreversible beyond a "point of no return". Although clinical antibiotic-based H. pylori eradication therapies reduce gastric cancer risk, their efficacy markedly diminishes once progressive gastric premalignant lesions developed, and long-term use often causes microbiome dysbiosis and antimicrobial resistance. To address these unmet clinical needs, we developed CurE-gel, an antibiotic-free smart in situ gel with pH- and lipase-cascade responsive drug release. This system enables targeted eradication of H. pylori while simultaneously facilitating gastric niche restoration. Composed of sodium alginate and polyacrylate, CurE-gel exhibits strong gastric mucosal adhesion and precise pH responsiveness. Utilizing the pathophysiological gastric pH gradient (luminal pH 1-2 vs. mucosal pH > 4), CurE-gel mediates unidirectional release of its encapsulated nanocapsules (CurE-cap) at the damaged mucosal side. Then, CurE-cap penetrates the mucus and accumulated at H. pylori colonies, where its polycaprolactone shell is hydrolyzed by bacterial lipase to release curcumin and eugenol. This system achieved: (i) targeted H. pylori eradication via biofilm disruption and virulence suppression; (ii) epithelial barrier protection and pathological progression suppression through virulence translocation inhibition, ROS scavenging, lipid peroxidation reduction and DNA damage mitigation; and (iii) gastric homeostasis restoration by recovery of tight junction proteins and gastric microbiota modulation. In vivo, CurE-gel achieved over 99% H. pylori eradication, reversed gastric progressive premalignant lesions and reconstructed a healthy gastric microbiota without systemic toxicity. By integrating mucoadhesive retention with pH- and lipase-cascade responsive drug release, this platform sets an innovative paradigm for two-pronged strategy in targeted H. pylori clearance and gastric homeostasis restoration, ultimately aiming to prevent gastric carcinogenesis.

title: Activation of KIF18B-MYC axis by autophagic CUL3 degradation promotes copper imbalance essential for gastric cancer progression.
abstract: Imbalance of copper homeostasis leads to cancer progression, while its molecular basis and treatment approaches in gastric cancer remain elusive. Herein, MYC proto-oncogene and kinesin family member 18 B (KIF18B) were identified as transcriptional suppressors of metallothionein (MT) genes, thereby driving copper-mediated aggressiveness and ferroptosis resistance in gastric cancer. Mechanistically, KIF18B was stabilized via p62-mediated autophagic degradation of E3 ubiquitin ligase cullin 3 (CUL3), which activated MYC via physical interaction to repress expression of copper storage genes MT2A and MT1X, resulting in elevation of free copper, subsequent up-regulation of pyruvate carboxylase (PC) and ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1), increase of tricarboxylic acid cycle for energy production, and decrease of ferroptosis in gastric cancer. KIF18B facilitated growth or aggressiveness and inhibited ferroptosis of gastric cancer cells via increasing MYC activity. An inhibitory peptide was established to block interplay between KIF18B and MYC, which suppressed growth, invasion, or metastasis and induced ferroptosis of gastric cancer. High KIF18B, MYC, PC, or FTH1 expression was associated with poor prognosis, while low CUL3, MT2A, or MT1X levels were linked to unfavorable outcome of gastric cancer patients. These findings suggest that activation of KIF18B‒MYC axis by autophagic CUL3 degradation promotes copper imbalance essential for gastric cancer progression.

title: Baseline Peripheral Neuropathy Predicts Clinically Significant Neuropathy During Paclitaxel Treatment Following Oxaliplatin-based Chemotherapy.
abstract: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is a common dose-limiting toxicity that adversely affects quality of life and treatment continuity of patients with malignancy. Although cumulative oxaliplatin exposure is a recognized risk factor for neurotoxicity, it remains unclear whether cumulative exposure or baseline neurological status better predicts clinically significant CIPN during subsequent paclitaxel treatment. This study aimed to identify predictors of clinically significant CIPN during paclitaxel therapy, focusing on the relative predictive value of cumulative oxaliplatin exposure and baseline CIPN. We retrospectively reviewed 76 patients with advanced gastric cancer who received paclitaxel-based second-line therapy after oxaliplatin-containing first-line chemotherapy. The primary endpoint was time to development of grade ≥2 CIPN, and the secondary endpoint was CIPN worsening. Cox proportional hazards and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with CIPN progression. Grade ≥2 CIPN developed in 34 patients (44.7%). Baseline CIPN (grade 1 vs. 0) independently predicted subsequent grade ≥2 CIPN (hazard ratio=4.23, 95% confidence interval=1.67-10.72; p=0.002; odds ratio=5.00, 95% confidence interval=1.58-15.80; p=0.006). In contrast, cumulative oxaliplatin dose was not associated with grade ≥2 CIPN or CIPN worsening. Kaplan-Meier analysis also showed no association between cumulative oxaliplatin dose and time to CIPN worsening, whereas higher serum albumin levels tended to be associated with a lower risk of CIPN progression. Baseline CIPN was a stronger predictor of clinically significant neuropathy during paclitaxel treatment than prior cumulative oxaliplatin exposure. Routine assessment of baseline neurological status before paclitaxel initiation may help identify patients at high risk for clinically significant CIPN and support individualized treatment and monitoring strategies.

title: γ-T3 Increases the Sensitization of Gastric Cancer Cells to OXA by a Regulation of ARHGAP29.
abstract: γ-Tocotrienol (γ-T3) exhibits potent anti-cancer effects in vitro and in vivo. Our previous study demonstrated that γ-T3 modulates autophagy activity in gastric cancer (GC) cells via the GSK-3β/β-Catenin pathway. In this study, we further explored whether γ-T3 also enhances the chemosensitivity of GC cells to oxaliplatin (OXA) by regulating ARHGAP29, and verified the direct binding between γ-T3 and ARHGAP29 as well as the physical interaction of ARHGAP29 with GSK-3β. We employed cell viability assays, flow cytometry, tumor cell spheroid formation assays, RT-qPCR, Western blot analysis, and stable overexpression transfection. Additionally, cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), and chloroquine (CQ) rescue CCK-8 assays were performed for molecular interaction and autophagy function verification; we established a xenografted tumor model using MKN45 cells in BALB/c nude mice (nu/nu). γ-T3 and OXA inhibited GC cell proliferation in vitro and in vivo, with a synergistic effect when combined (CI = 0.55 in MKN45 cells). In a mouse model, intraperitoneal injection of γ-T3 (20 mg/kg b.w.) and OXA (2.0 mg/kg b.w.) suppressed MKN45 cell xenograft growth. This was related to cell cycle arrest and inhibition of cancer stem cells (CSCs). γ-T3 alone or combined with OXA altered autophagy-related protein levels after 48 h treatment, with elevated LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and Beclin1 expression, and reduced p62 abundance, functional rescue with autophagy inhibitor CQ confirmed that the changed autophagy contributes to drug-induced cell death, and this phenotypic change was accompanied by suppressed GSK-3β/β-Catenin pathway activity. ARHGAP29 was inversely correlated with GC prognosis; CETSA results validated the direct intracellular binding between γ-T3 and ARHGAP29, and Co-IP assays confirmed physical interaction between ARHGAP29 and GSK-3β. γ-T3 inhibited the expression of ARHGAP29 at protein and mRNA levels in a time- and dose-dependent manner, whether alone or with OXA. Overexpression of ARHGAP29 reversed the synergistic effects of γ-T3 and OXA in GC cells, further supporting the regulatory linkage between ARHGAP29 and the GSK-3β/β-Catenin axis. The combination of γ-T3 and OXA represents a promising therapeutic strategy to elevate oxaliplatin sensitivity and alter autophagy-related marker expression in GC, at least partially via the ARHGAP29-associated modulation of GSK-3β/β-Catenin signaling.
journal: Journal of biochemical and molecular toxicology

title: Gastric Cancer: Epidemiology, Risk Factors, Pathogenesis, Clinical Features, Diagnosis, and Management.
abstract: Gastric cancer is a multifactorial disease shaped by diverse risk factors and a complex pathogenesis spanning from chronic atrophic gastritis to invasive malignancy. Its global incidence shows marked geographic disparities, and advances in understanding its pathogenic mechanisms have improved diagnosis and treatment. Although the relationship between gastric cancer and macrophages has been extensively investigated, a systematic review integrating the entire clinical and biological continuum of gastric cancer, from epidemiology to management, with a focus on macrophages remains lacking. This review summarizes the epidemiology and multidimensional risk factors for gastric cancer, including infectious, dietary, genetic, microbiome, and metabolite-related factors. We describe the evolution of precancerous conditions, molecular alterations such as miRNA expression, and the bidirectional interactions between gastric cancer cells and macrophages that drive tumor progression within the tumor microenvironment. We also review clinical features, diagnostic approaches based on screening and endoscopy, and current management strategies, including surgery, systemic therapies, targeted therapies, immunotherapy, macrophage-targeted therapies, macrophage metabolic reprogramming, and recent preclinical and clinical advances. Overall, this review integrates evidence from epidemiology, molecular biology, immunology, and pathology to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding gastric cancer pathogenesis and current as well as emerging therapeutic strategies.

title: Surgical Procedure and Postoperative S-1 Chemotherapy Deliverability in Symptomatic Stage IV Gastric Cancer.
abstract: Symptomatic incurable stage IV gastric cancer (GC) may require palliative surgery for bleeding or obstruction before systemic therapy. We examined whether procedure type-distal gastrectomy (DG), total gastrectomy (TG), or gastrojejunostomy (GJ)-is associated with nutritional/inflammatory changes, S-1 deliverability, and overall survival (OS). We retrospectively studied 49 patients who underwent palliative DG (n=13), TG (n=20), or GJ (n=16) and then received S-1 as first-line postoperative chemotherapy. Body weight, prognostic nutritional index (PNI), and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) were assessed preoperatively and before chemotherapy. Deliverability was evaluated by time to S-1 initiation, continuation beyond 3 months, and treatment modification within 3 months. OS was analyzed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox models. Postoperative complications were more frequent after GJ (p=0.002); time to S-1 initiation was similar among groups (p=0.144). S-1 continuation beyond 3 months was achieved in 29/49 patients (59.2%; DG 76.9%, TG 55.0%, GJ 50.0%; p=0.302). Weight loss was significantly greater after TG than after DG or GJ, and GJ showed a postoperative decline in PNI and a significantly higher pre-chemotherapy NLR than DG and TG (p=0.015 and p=0.036, respectively). Median OS was 474 days (DG: 812, TG: 422, and GJ: 293 days) and was significantly longer after DG than after TG (p=0.042) or GJ (p=0.003). In multivariate Cox analysis, chemotherapy for ≥3 months (HR=0.46, 95% CI=0.22-0.95; p=0.036) and high PNI (HR=0.31, 95% CI=0.13-0.77; p=0.012) were independent prognostic factors. In symptomatic incurable stage IV GC treated with palliative surgery followed by S-1, procedure type was associated with distinct perioperative profiles and OS. Maintaining chemotherapy and immuno-nutritional status may be clinically relevant in these patients.

title: Association of Recurrence-free Interval With Survival After Recurrence in Gastric Cancer: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.
abstract: The prognostic significance of recurrence-free interval (RFI) after gastrectomy in patients with gastric cancer (GC) remains unclear, and previous studies have reported inconsistent associations between the timing of recurrence and survival after recurrence. This study evaluated the association of RFI with post-recurrence overall survival (OS) and recurrence patterns in patients receiving first-line chemotherapy for recurrent GC. This multicenter retrospective study included 190 patients who underwent R0 gastrectomy and subsequently received first-line chemotherapy for recurrence between January 2015 and September 2025. RFI was analyzed as a log-transformed continuous variable and its association with post-recurrence OS was evaluated using multivariable Cox regression and restricted cubic spline models. Patients were classified into three groups according to RFI (<6, 6-12, and ≥12 months) for descriptive analyses of patient characteristics and recurrence patterns. The prevalence of peritoneal recurrence increased across the three RFI groups (25.9%, 56.4%, and 56.5%, respectively; p=0.013). Multivariable analysis identified longer log-transformed RFI as independently associated with higher mortality risk [hazard ratio (HR)=1.42, 95% confidence interval (CI)=1.18-1.71; p<0.001]. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status ≥1 (HR=2.63, 95%CI=1.82-3.80; p<0.001), peritoneal recurrence (HR=2.06, 95%CI=1.45-2.91; p<0.001), and prognostic nutritional index (HR=0.95, 95%CI=0.92-0.98; p<0.001) were also independently associated with post-recurrence OS. There was a significant overall association between RFI and post-recurrence OS (p=0.0012), with no significant evidence of nonlinearity (p=0.18). The findings remained consistent after adjusting for treatment period, adjuvant chemotherapy, and first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor use. A longer log-transformed RFI was independently associated with higher mortality risk in patients receiving first-line chemotherapy for recurrent GC after gastrectomy. Prognostic assessment after recurrence should consider RFI together with performance status, nutritional status, and recurrence pattern.

title: Crystal structure of tyrosine-tRNA synthetase from Helicobacter pylori G27.
abstract: Helicobacter pylori, a major cause of gastric ulcers and cancers, infects nearly half of the world's population. The crystal structure of a potential H. pylori structure-guided drug-discovery target, tyrosine-tRNA synthetase (HpTyrRS), has been determined by the Seattle Structural Genomics Center for Infectious Disease (SSGCID). HpTyrRS is an enzyme that catalyzes the ATP-dependent attachment of tyrosine to tRNA. HpTyrRS was produced and crystallized, and its structure was determined at 2.2 Å resolution. HpTyrRS has a prototypical bacterial TyrRS topology and forms dimers in solution. HpTyrRS shares a conserved binding cavity for a previously identified Staphylococcus aureus TyrRS inhibitor (SB-219383). The reported structure and analysis establish HpTyrRS as a potential target for structure-guided drug discovery and repurposing.
journal: Acta crystallographica. Section F, Structural biology communications

title: Autoimmune gastritides: A critical review.
abstract: Autoimmune gastritis (AIG) has long been considered a host-related autoimmune disease that results in oxyntic atrophy, leading to Pernicious Anemia and increasing neoplastic risk. Current evidence discloses that gastric autoimmunity includes a spectrum of inflammatory diseases (i.e., Autoimmune Gastritides) with distinct etiologies, comorbidities, clinical presentations, histological phenotypes, and outcomes. To distinguish the clinical-pathological subtypes of immunomediated gastric disorders. Gastric autoimmune diseases comprise Type-1 and Type-2 variants. Type-1 atrophic AIG may lead to vitamin B12 malabsorption, resulting in pernicious anemia, and carries a high risk of Type-1 neuroendocrine gastric neoplasia. Type-1a AIG includes two subtypes. Type-1a is the canonical oxyntic-restricted AIG subtype with no history of exposure to H. pylori infection. In this subtype, a T-cell-rich, cytolytic infiltrate targets the corpus/fundus mucosa, resulting in oxyntic-restricted atrophic changes. Type-1b combines autoimmune etiology with prior or current exposure to H. pylori infection. The dual etiology of Type-1b AIG combines autoimmune oxyntic damage with H. pylori-related antral lesions. This condition may lead to extensive (antral and oxyntic) atrophy, necessitating cancer prevention strategies tailored to the histological stage of gastritis. Type-2 AIG is far less frequent than Type-1, presents with mucus-secreting (antral-pyloric) and oxyntic (corpus/fundus) erosive mucosal high-grade pangastritis, and involves symptomatic multiorgan immune-mediated comorbidities, irrespective of H. pylori status. Type-2 combines Type-1-like serology with a wide, variable spectrum of circulating organ-specific and non-organ-specific autoantibodies and requires targeted treatment. The nosology of autoimmune gastritides should reflect their diverse etio-pathogenesis, clinicopathological presentations, and outcomes.

title: METTL3-mediated m⁶A methylation of E2F2 targets MCU to promote the malignant phenotype of gastric cancer cells.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is a highly prevalent malignancy worldwide, and its progression is closely linked to aberrant epigenetic regulation. E2F transcription factor 2 (E2F2), a member of the E2F transcription factor family, has been identified as an oncogene in various cancers. However, the regulatory effects of epigenetic modifications on E2F2 in GC remain incompletely clarified. To address this knowledge gap, the current study was designed to elucidate the impact of Methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3)-mediated N⁶-methyladenosine (m⁶A) methylation of E2F2 on mitochondrial function in GC cells by regulating the mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU). Both in vitro and in vivo analyses revealed a critical oncogenic axis in GC driven by METTL3. This axis, mediated by m⁶A modification, post-transcriptionally stabilizes E2F2 mRNA, resulting in the upregulation of MCU expression and consequent aberrant mitochondrial calcium uptake. Functional assays revealed that activation of the METTL3/E2F2/MCU axis promotes GC cell proliferation and migration and inhibits apoptosis, whereas knockdown of METTL3 or E2F2 reverses these malignant phenotypes. Mechanistically, METTL3 binds to the 3' untranslated region of E2F2 mRNA to enhance its stability, and E2F2 in turn transcriptionally activates MCU expression. Clinical data analysis indicated positive correlations among METTL3, E2F2, and MCU expression, with high levels associated with poor patient prognosis. These findings suggest that targeting the m⁶A modification pathway holds promise for GC therapy, as the newly identified METTL3-E2F2-MCU axis plays a key role in regulating mitochondrial calcium homeostasis.

title: PCK1 promotes gastric cancer progression by activating the SRC1-JAK1-STAT3 signaling axis.
abstract: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1) has been shown to have signalling functions beyond gluconeogenesis. However, its role in gastric cancer is unclear. To determine the clinical significance, biological function and molecular mechanism of PCK1 in gastric cancer. PCK1 expression and prognostic value were evaluated using public databases and validated in gastric cancer tissues and cell lines. The effects of PCK1 knockdown in AGS and HGC-27 cells were assessed using CCK-8, colony formation, Transwell and wound-healing assays. The underlying mechanism was investigated using transcriptomic analysis, protein interaction analysis, qRT-PCR, Western blotting, co-immunoprecipitation, SRC1 rescue experiments and nude-mouse xenograft models. The associations between PCK1 and the tumour immune microenvironment were also analysed. PCK1 was found to be upregulated in gastric cancer and to be associated with a poor prognosis. Knockdown of PCK1 suppressed cell viability, clonogenicity, migration, invasion and xenograft growth, reduced Ki-67 expression and increased cleaved caspase-3 expression. PCK1 formed a protein complex with SRC1; however, its knockdown decreased SRC1 expression, as well as JAK1 and STAT3 phosphorylation and PD-L1 expression. SRC1 overexpression partially reversed these molecular and phenotypic effects. PCK1 expression was associated with immune cell infiltration but showed no clear relationship with the overall TIDE score or predicted immunotherapy response. PCK1 promotes gastric cancer progression partly through the SRC1/JAK1/STAT3 axis and regulation of PD-L1, suggesting its potential as a therapeutic target. However, its immunomodulatory and predictive value requires further validation.

title: Multifaceted roles of chemokines in gastric cancer: From tumor microenvironment modulation to therapeutic targeting (Review).
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is a malignant solid tumor with limited treatment options, particularly for advanced tumor stages. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T therapy has been successful in treating hematological malignancies; however, its efficacy in solid tumors remains suboptimal due to the complex tumor microenvironment (TME). The TME in GC comprises diverse signaling molecules and cellular components, including fibroblasts, immune cells and stromal proteins; these components can support tumor growth, invasion and immune evasion. In the GC TME, the dynamic interactions between cytokines, chemokines, growth factors and their receptors can foster chronic inflammation and immunosuppression, thereby facilitating tumor progression, metastasis and therapeutic resistance. The present review provides novel insights into the understanding and functional impact of cell-chemokine interaction networks in GC, highlighting the therapeutic implications of chemokines in immunotherapy. In addition, current related research areas are outlined and advances in therapeutic strategies targeting key chemokine signaling pathways are discussed. By providing critical insights into TME reprogramming and immunomodulation, the current study aims to encourage the strategic application of chemokine engineering in next-generation CAR-T immunotherapy for GC.

title: Pharmacotherapy for older adults with cancer: a digest of the Japanese clinical practice guidelines (2nd edition)-gastrointestinal cancers.
abstract: The number of older adults with gastrointestinal cancers is increasing in rapidly aging societies. However, optimal pharmacotherapy for this population remains challenging because of heterogeneity in functional status, comorbidities, and the limited representation of older patients in clinical trials. This article presents an English digest of the Japanese Clinical Practice Guidelines for Pharmacotherapy in Older Adults with Cancer (second edition) [5] with a focus on gastrointestinal cancers. The guidelines were developed in accordance with the Minds 2020 methodology, incorporating systematic reviews, the Evidence-to-Decision framework, and multidisciplinary consensus. The guideline addresses key clinical questions regarding systemic therapy for older patients with gastric and colorectal cancers, including combination chemotherapy, biomarker-guided therapy, and adjuvant treatment strategies. All recommendations were conditional because of limited direct evidence in older populations. Specifically, in gastric cancer, oxaliplatin-containing combination therapy and biomarker-guided treatment may be considered for appropriately selected patients and are conditionally recommended. In colorectal cancer, routine treatment intensification with oxaliplatin- or irinotecan-containing regimens is not uniformly recommended. Treatment decisions should be individualized by weighing the expected benefit against the risk of increased toxicity, particularly in frail or very old patients. These guidelines provide practical evidence-informed recommendations for pharmacotherapy in older adults with gastrointestinal cancers. They emphasize individualized treatment strategies that integrate patient characteristics, treatment goals, and tolerability. Further research, specifically targeting older populations, is required to strengthen the evidence base in geriatric oncology.

title: Lactylation in gastric cancer: From mechanisms to clinical applications (Review).
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is one of the most common malignant tumors worldwide. Metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic dysregulation represent its key pathological characteristics. As a novel lactate‑mediated post‑translational modification, lactylation converts metabolic signals into epigenetic and protein functional regulation, and it is extensively and aberrantly activated in GC. Lactylation drives the malignant progression of GC by promoting cell proliferation, invasion, metastasis and stemness. In addition, lactylation suppresses antitumor immune cell functions, and mediates immune escape and therapeutic resistance. Clinically, global lactylation levels and specific lactylation sites can serve as independent prognostic biomarkers, and corresponding risk models enable prognostic stratification and prediction of immunotherapy response. Intervention strategies targeting lactate production, lactyltransferases and downstream effector axes have emerged as promising directions for GC treatment. The present review summarizes the regulatory mechanisms, biological functions and clinical translational value of lactylation in GC, aiming to provide novel insights for precision diagnostics and therapeutics.

title: Long non-coding RNA GAS6-AS1 and its molecular mechanisms in human cancer (Review).
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) play crucial roles in regulating gene expression and tumor progression. Growth arrest specific 6-antisense RNA 1 (GAS6-AS1), a novel lncRNA located antisense to the GAS6 gene, has been increasingly recognized as an important regulator in multiple cancers. Emerging evidence demonstrates that GAS6-AS1 participates in tumor initiation and progression by functioning as a competitive endogenous RNA that modulates microRNA activity, regulates downstream target genes, and influences key signaling pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin and AXL signaling. Through these mechanisms, GAS6-AS1 affects cancer cell proliferation, migration, invasion, apoptosis, metabolic reprogramming and chemoresistance. GAS6-AS1 exhibits context-dependent functions across different cancer types. GAS6-AS1 predominantly functions as an oncogenic lncRNA in multiple cancers, including colorectal cancer, breast cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, ovarian cancer, glioma, gastric cancer, renal cell carcinoma and acute myeloid leukemia. In contrast, GAS6-AS1 has been reported to exert tumor-suppressive effects in lung adenocarcinoma. Abnormal expression of GAS6-AS1 is closely associated with tumor progression, metastasis and patient prognosis, highlighting its potential as a diagnostic and prognostic biomarker as well as a therapeutic target. Overall, GAS6-AS1 represents a promising molecule for understanding cancer pathogenesis and developing novel strategies for precision cancer diagnosis and treatment, although further clinical validation and mechanistic studies are still required.

title: ASO Author Reflections: Proximal Gastrectomy After Neoadjuvant Therapy: Function-Preserving Surgery for Gastroesophageal Junction Cancer.
Assessing the efficacy of adjuvant chemotherapy in patients with T3N0 gastric cancer.
abstract: Adjuvant chemotherapy is standard for advanced gastric cancer based on randomized controlled trials. However, its effectiveness in patients with T3N0 stage, who were not included in these trials, remains unclear. This study assessed its clinical benefits by comparing outcomes between patients with T3N0 stage who received postoperative chemotherapy with those who did not. From 2011 to 2019, a retrospective analysis was performed on 386 patients with pathologically diagnosed T3N0 advanced gastric cancer who underwent radical gastrectomy. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to analyze overall survival(OS) and relapse-free survival (RFS) between groups. Among 386 patients, 188 received adjuvant chemotherapy and 198 underwent surgery alone. After IPTW adjustment, the 5-year OS were 93.1 % in the adjuvant chemotherapy group and 91.3 % in the surgery-only group, and the 5-year RFS were 88.4 % and 84.4 %, respectively. Adjuvant chemotherapy was not associated with a significant reduction in the risk of death (hazard ratio [HR], 0.72; 95 % confidence interval [CI], 0.32-1.61; P = 0.428) or recurrence (HR, 0.68; 95 % CI, 0.34-1.34; P = 0.264). Overall recurrence rates and recurrence patterns were comparable between the two groups after adjustment. Among patients who received chemotherapy, grade III/IV adverse events occurred in 26.7 % of those treated with TS-1 and 70.4 % of those treated with XELOX. In patients with T3N0 stage after surgery, the chemotherapy group demonstrated OS and RFS similar to surgery-only group. Therefore, the benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy in patients with T3N0 gastric cancer remains uncertain.
journal: European journal of surgical oncology : the journal of the European Society of Surgical Oncology and the British Association of Surgical Oncology
